COPPERLEAF DENTAL GROUP: ACCOUNTS PAYABLE POLICY
Document AP-001, Revision 7 (current)
Effective: 1 February 2024
Owner: Dalia Bergstrom, Finance Controller
Supersedes: AP-001 Revision 6 and every sticky note on the monitor in the back office

A NOTE BEFORE YOU SCROLL PAST THIS

We know. Nobody reads policy pages. People skim for their own name, find it missing, and go back to emailing invoices to whichever finance person they last had lunch with. This is the seventh revision of this document, and we have been told the first six were "very thorough." That is the phrase people use for things they did not read. This revision is shorter than Revision 6 by about eleven words. We consider that progress.

If you are a clinic manager, a practice owner, a regional operations lead, or anyone else who has ever said "just pay it, I'll sort the paperwork later," this page is for you. If you are a vendor who found this page, welcome. Please read Section 4 twice.

SECTION 1: PURPOSE

This policy describes how Copperleaf Dental Group receives, checks, approves, records and pays supplier invoices. It exists so that we pay the right supplier, the right amount, once, on time, and with enough documentation that an auditor does not have to ask us the same question three times. It also exists so that the finance team can take a lunch break without discovering on return that someone has wired a deposit to a laboratory that went out of business in 2019.

The goals, in no particular order of how often we fail at them:

1. Pay valid invoices by their due date under the terms in Section 6.
2. Never pay an invoice twice. Once is plenty.
3. Never pay for goods or services we did not order or did not receive.
4. Keep a clean record for tax, audit and the occasional suspicious practice owner.
5. Take early-payment discounts when they are actually worth taking, and only then.

SECTION 2: SCOPE

This policy applies to all Copperleaf Dental Group entities, including all eighteen clinics, the central sterilization facility in Morrow Park, the two orthodontic satellite offices, and the regional head office, which despite its name is mostly a conference room and a coffee machine with opinions.

It covers invoices for dental supplies, laboratory work, equipment purchases and leases, facilities maintenance, IT services, professional services, marketing, cleaning, courier and waste removal, and anything else that arrives with a number at the bottom and the word "due" somewhere near it.

It does not cover employee expense reimbursements (see Policy EX-003, which is somehow longer than this one), payroll, patient refunds (see Policy PR-010), or intercompany charges between Copperleaf entities (see the Group Accounting Manual, Chapter 9, which nobody has opened since it was printed).

SECTION 3: VENDOR ONBOARDING

Before any supplier can be paid, the supplier must exist in the vendor master file. "Exist" here means something more than "a clinic manager has their mobile number."

To be set up, a new vendor must provide:

- A completed Copperleaf Vendor Information Form.
- A W-9 (or the equivalent tax form for non-US suppliers).
- Bank details on company letterhead, signed, and confirmed by a call-back to a phone number we obtained independently. Not the number printed on the letterhead. Not the number in the email signature. A number we found ourselves, like adults.
- A certificate of insurance where the vendor will perform work on our premises.

Please note that the W-9 is an onboarding document. It is collected once when the vendor is set up and refreshed every three years. It is not part of the invoice matching process described in Section 5 and should not be stapled to every invoice. We have received, to date, four hundred and twelve stapled W-9s. We are keeping them as a monument.

Changes to vendor bank details follow the same call-back rule. Any email that says "we have changed banks, please update" is treated as fraudulent until proven otherwise. Last year one such email was written in impeccable English, had the correct logo, and came from a domain that differed from the real vendor's by one letter. It was very convincing. It was also a crime.

SECTION 4: HOW INVOICES REACH US

All supplier invoices must be sent to the central inbox, invoices@copperleaf-ap.example, as a PDF attachment, one invoice per PDF. Paper invoices mailed to clinics should be scanned and forwarded to the same inbox by the clinic within two business days of receipt.

Invoices must show:

- The Copperleaf entity being billed.
- A valid Copperleaf purchase order number for anything that required a PO (see Section 5).
- An invoice number that is unique for that vendor.
- Invoice date, due date or payment terms, and a clear total with tax shown separately.

Invoices sent to individual staff members, to the CEO's personal address, to the clinic's general enquiries inbox, or "left at reception with the lady with the nice glasses" are not considered received until they reach the central inbox. The payment clock under Section 6 starts from the date the invoice arrives in the central inbox, not from the date printed on it, and certainly not from the date the vendor says they "definitely sent it."

Vendors: we understand that you have a preferred contact at our clinics and that the preferred contact is lovely. The preferred contact cannot pay you. Only the central inbox can start that process.

SECTION 5: PURCHASE ORDERS AND THE THREE-WAY MATCH

Purchases of goods and services at or above $500 require a purchase order raised in the procurement system before the purchase is made. "Before" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. A PO raised after the invoice arrives is called an after-the-fact PO, and it is flagged in the monthly exception report with a little red icon that we are told makes people feel bad. Good.

For PO-backed invoices, Accounts Payable performs a three-way match before an invoice can be approved for payment. The three documents are:

1. The purchase order, showing what was ordered, the quantity, and the agreed price.
2. The receiving report, entered in the procurement system by the clinic or facility that took delivery, confirming what actually arrived and in what quantity.
3. The vendor invoice, showing what the vendor is charging us.

All three must agree within tolerance: quantity must match exactly, and unit price must be within 2% or $50 of the PO price, whichever is lower. If they do not match, the invoice goes on hold and the requester is notified.

Things that are NOT part of the three-way match, despite the enthusiasm with which people send them:

- Packing slips. A packing slip is a piece of paper the vendor put in the box. It is not a receiving report. You may photograph it if it gives you joy, and it can help you fill in the receiving report accurately, but AP does not require it and will not hold an invoice for lack of one.
- The vendor contract or master service agreement. Contracts matter; they set the prices that go on the PO. But once the PO exists, AP matches against the PO, not the contract. Please do not attach a forty-page MSA to a $612 invoice for gloves.
- The W-9. See Section 3. See the monument.
- A screenshot of a text message from the sales rep saying "it's fine, just pay it."

Invoices below $500 without a PO may be approved on a two-way basis (invoice plus confirmation of receipt from the requester), provided the vendor is in the vendor master file and the requester has budget authority. Splitting a $1,400 purchase into three invoices of $466.67 to stay under the PO threshold is not clever. It is visible. We have a report for it. The report has a name, and the name is yours.

SECTION 6: PAYMENT TERMS

Unless a different term has been agreed in writing and recorded in the vendor master file, Copperleaf's standard payment term is net 45 days from the date the invoice is received in the central inbox.

Some vendors have negotiated terms different from the standard. These are exceptions and they are recorded individually in the vendor master file. At the time of this revision, recorded exceptions include:

- Harbor Freight (maintenance tools and shop supplies for the sterilization facility): net 30, agreed in 2023 in exchange for volume pricing.
- Our primary dental laboratory partner: net 60, under the lab services agreement.
- Utilities and statutory payments: paid by the stated due date regardless of the standard term.

The existence of these exceptions does not change the standard term for everyone else. We say this because at least three clinic managers have told vendors that "Copperleaf pays in 30 days" after seeing the Harbor Freight arrangement mentioned in a meeting. Copperleaf pays in 45 days. Harbor Freight gets 30. You are not Harbor Freight. Neither is the vendor you are talking to.

Payment runs occur every Tuesday and Thursday. An invoice is paid in the last payment run on or before its due date, not earlier, unless Section 7 applies.

SECTION 7: EARLY-PAYMENT DISCOUNTS

We like free money. We are not fools about it.

Where a vendor offers a discount for early payment (for example "2/10 net 45," meaning 2% off if paid within 10 days), AP will take the discount only if both of the following are true:

(a) The discount is at least 1.5% of the invoice total; and
(b) The invoice has cleared matching and approval early enough to be paid inside the discount window.

If the discount is smaller than 1.5%, we do not take it; it is not worth the cash-flow cost and the manual handling. If the invoice is stuck on a matching hold because someone forgot to enter a receiving report, we do not take it either, and the lost discount appears in the monthly exception report next to the requester's name. We are not saying this to shame anyone. We are saying it to shame someone specific, who knows who they are.

In short: early-payment discounts are taken when they meet the threshold and the invoice is ready in time. They are not taken automatically, and they are not taken because a vendor underlines them in red.

SECTION 8: APPROVAL AUTHORITY

Once matched, invoices require approval according to the invoice total (including tax) as follows:

- Up to and including $2,500: the requesting clinic manager or department head.
- Above $2,500 and up to and including $25,000: the Finance Controller (currently Dalia Bergstrom), after the clinic manager or department head has confirmed the business need.
- Above $25,000: the Chief Financial Officer, after Finance Controller review.

Approvers may not approve invoices for purchases they personally requested above $2,500; such invoices move to the next level up. Approvers may not approve invoices from vendors in which they or a family member hold an interest. You would be surprised how often we need to write that sentence down. Actually, you would not.

Approval by email reply is accepted only from the approver's own Copperleaf mailbox. Approval forwarded by an assistant, pasted into a chat message, or "said out loud in the corridor" is not approval.

Delegation: an approver going on leave may delegate authority to someone at the same level or higher, in writing, for a defined period. Delegating to "whoever is around" is not a defined period or a defined person.

SECTION 9: DUPLICATE INVOICES

The system flags possible duplicates when the vendor, amount and invoice date match, or when the vendor and invoice number match. Flagged invoices are held until AP confirms they are genuinely separate. Vendors who resend the same invoice with "COPY" or "REMINDER" written across the top should know that we can read, and that the original is already in the queue.

If you notice that an invoice has been paid twice, tell AP immediately. Do not "just ask the vendor to take it off the next one." The vendor will agree with enormous warmth and then forget.

SECTION 10: DISPUTES AND HOLDS

If an invoice is incorrect, the requester or AP raises a dispute with the vendor within 10 business days of identifying the problem. The disputed portion is placed on hold; the undisputed portion may be paid on normal terms if the vendor agrees to a partial payment. The payment term for the disputed portion restarts on receipt of a corrected invoice or credit note.

SECTION 11: LATE FEES AND INTEREST

Copperleaf does not agree to late fees in vendor terms unless the CFO approves them in writing. Late fees that appear on invoices without such agreement are disputed under Section 10. Late fees caused by our own delay (for example, an invoice sitting in a clinic drawer for three weeks) are charged to the budget of the clinic responsible. The drawer does not have a budget. The clinic does.

SECTION 12: YEAR-END CUT-OFF

For the financial year end, all invoices for goods or services received on or before the last day of the year must reach the central inbox by the fifth business day of the new year, and all receiving reports must be entered by the same date. Goods received but not invoiced by then are accrued based on the PO and receiving report. The practice of "holding invoices until January so the budget looks better" is noticed every year, by the same people, who write the same email about it.

SECTION 13: QUESTIONS

Questions about this policy go to the AP team through the central inbox with "Policy question" in the subject line. Questions about why the policy exists go to the history section in Appendix A. Complaints about the tone of this policy go to the same inbox and will be read with the seriousness they deserve.

APPENDIX A: REVISION HISTORY (FOR REFERENCE ONLY; NOT CURRENT POLICY)

The following summarizes earlier revisions. It is included because people keep quoting them to us as though they were still in force. They are not. Please stop.

Revision 4 (2019): Standard payment term was net 60. Approval limits were: clinic managers up to $1,000; regional operations leads up to $10,000; CFO above $10,000. There was no Finance Controller role. There was also no three-way match; AP matched the invoice to the PO only, which is how we paid for the same autoclave twice.

Revision 5 (2021): Standard term moved to net 30 for a trial period of one year, after which it was abandoned because cash flow looked, in the CFO's words, "like a crime scene." Three-way match introduced.

Revision 6 (2022): Standard term set to net 45. Approval limits were: clinic managers and department heads up to $5,000; Finance Controller from $5,000.01 to $50,000; CFO above $50,000. Early-payment discounts were taken automatically regardless of size, which produced one memorable month in which we accelerated $180,000 of payments to save $412.

Revision 7 (2024, current): Approval limits lowered as set out in Section 8 following the internal audit recommendation. Early-payment discount threshold introduced (Section 7). Packing slip and W-9 clarifications added because apparently they were needed.

APPENDIX B: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

Q: My clinic ordered $3,000 of composite materials. I'm the clinic manager. Can I approve the invoice?
A: No. Under Section 8, $3,000 is above $2,500, so it goes to the Finance Controller after you confirm the business need. Under Revision 6 you could have approved it yourself, which is exactly why Revision 6 is no longer in force.

Q: The vendor says Copperleaf pays in 30 days. Is that right?
A: Only if the vendor is Harbor Freight, or has its own recorded exception. Otherwise it is net 45. See Section 6. Also see Appendix A, where you will find the net 30 trial that we would all prefer to forget.

Q: The vendor offers 1% off if we pay within 10 days. Will AP take it?
A: No. 1% is below the 1.5% threshold in Section 7.

Q: I attached the packing slip, the W-9 and the MSA. Why is my invoice still on hold?
A: Because the receiving report is missing. The receiving report is the one we need. The others are souvenirs.

Q: I found an old laminated card in the supply room that says clinic managers can approve up to $5,000. Is it still valid?
A: It is valid as a coaster.

Q: A vendor emailed to say their bank details changed. They sounded really nice.
A: So do most fraudsters. Call-back procedure, Section 3.

APPENDIX C: EXAMPLE WORKED CASE

Order: Clinic 11 raises PO 11-4402 for 40 boxes of nitrile gloves at $14.50 per box, total $580.00.
Delivery: 40 boxes arrive; the clinic enters a receiving report for 40.
Invoice: The vendor invoices 40 boxes at $14.75 per box, total $590.00, terms 2/10 net 45.
Match: quantity matches; unit price differs by $0.25, which is 1.7% of $14.50 and $10 in total, within tolerance (2% or $50, whichever is lower). Match passes.
Approval: $590.00 is under $2,500; clinic manager approves.
Discount: 2% is at least 1.5%, and the invoice cleared on day 4, so AP pays on the next payment run inside the 10-day window and takes $11.80 off.
If the clinic had forgotten the receiving report until day 12, the discount would be lost and would appear on the exception report, and the clinic manager would receive a polite email that is less polite than it sounds.

End of document. Congratulations on reaching the end. You are in a small and distinguished group.

Uma, forwarding Sven's update since you asked who's "on hold" and I refuse to answer from memory; scroll down, it's riveting.

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Sven Fischer
To: Xiu Sorensen
Cc: Kwame Rahman
Date: Friday 8 March, 17:52
Subject: AP weekly status, week ending 8 March

Hi Xiu,

Here is the weekly accounts payable status for Quill Dental. I have tried to keep it short. I have failed, because the week was not short. It was, by my count, roughly nine weeks long, compressed into five days, most of them spent explaining to people that an invoice is not paid just because they looked at it with intent.

Headline numbers first, since I know you read those and then skip to the part where I complain.

SUMMARY

- Invoices received this week: 214 (last week: 187).
- Invoices processed and approved: 196.
- Invoices paid in the Tuesday and Thursday runs: 181, totalling $412,660.18.
- Invoices currently on hold: 23 (details below, with the vendors that actually matter called out by name).
- Open disputes: 6, of which three are worth your attention and three are worth nobody's attention, including the vendors'.
- Days payable outstanding: 41, down from 43. Nobody will thank us for this. I am thanking us now.

If you want the version where everything is fine, stop reading here. Everything is fine. Several things are also on fire. Both can be true.

1. LARKSPUR RENTALS: THE GREAT DOUBLE INVOICE

Larkspur Rentals, who supply the portable X-ray units and the compressor rentals at the three east-side clinics, sent us invoice LR-4471 on 26 February for $8,420.00, covering February rental of the compressors plus a "delivery and calibration surcharge." On 4 March they sent LR-4471A for the same amount, same period, same line items, with the word "REVISED" at the top. The only thing revised, as far as I can tell, is the letter A.

The duplicate check caught it on Tuesday morning before the payment run. Neither LR-4471 nor LR-4471A has been paid. I want to be very clear about that, because by Wednesday afternoon at least two clinic managers had told each other that "Larkspur got paid twice," and by Thursday one of them had told Larkspur's account rep, who emailed me in a mild panic offering to refund money we never sent. I thanked her for her generosity and explained that we cannot accept a refund of a payment that does not exist, as appealing as it sounds.

On top of the duplicate, we are disputing the full $8,420.00 on the original. The delivery and calibration surcharge of $1,900.00 is not on the PO; the rental agreement says calibration is included. And the compressor count on the invoice is six, while the receiving report and the PO both say four. Rather than try to pay a partial amount on an invoice that is wrong in two places, I have put the whole of LR-4471 on hold pending a corrected invoice, and I have rejected LR-4471A outright as a duplicate.

Status: Larkspur Rentals is on payment hold. Dispute value: $8,420.00. Corrected invoice requested Tuesday. Larkspur's rep says the corrected invoice will be with us "early next week," which I have translated into my calendar as "at some point."

2. TAMSIN OFFICE SUPPLY: THE PAPER MOUNTAIN

Tamsin Office Supply invoiced $11,900.00 on 20 February for the quarterly bulk order: paper, toner, patient intake clipboards, and approximately one million pens, of which I suspect half have already vanished into the pockets of patients.

This is the largest single invoice in our current queue that has been disputed, and I know that number will be the one people remember, so let me head it off: we are not disputing $11,900.00. We are disputing $3,150.00 of it, which is the toner line. They billed us for 90 toner cartridges; the receiving reports from the clinics add up to 45. The other $8,750.00 was matched and approved and paid in Tuesday's run, with Tamsin's written agreement to a partial payment.

The disputed $3,150.00 was on hold. It is not on hold any more. On Thursday, Tamsin sent a credit note for the 45 missing cartridges, reducing the toner line to $1,575.00, which I matched against the receiving reports, and I lifted the hold at 11:20 on Thursday. The remaining $1,575.00 will go in Tuesday's run. So Tamsin is off hold and the dispute is closed. I mention it here only because it will still show as "recently held" on the dashboard until the weekly refresh, and I would rather you heard it from me than from the dashboard, which has no sense of nuance.

3. BRIGHTWATER COURIER: THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY GOT PAID TWICE

Here is the one that deserves the gossip Larkspur has been getting.

Brightwater Courier, our specimen and lab-work courier, invoiced us $1,280.00 for February. That invoice was paid in the 27 February run. Brightwater then sent the same invoice again under a new invoice number, BWC-2024-0233 instead of BWC-2024-0219, with a different invoice date. Because the invoice number and the date were both different, our duplicate check, which looks for matching vendor plus matching number, or matching vendor plus amount plus date, did not flag it. It was approved by a clinic manager who, in fairness, had no reason to remember the first one, and it went out in the 5 March run.

So yes: we paid Brightwater $1,280.00 twice. The second payment went out on Tuesday 5 March. It has cleared. It is, in the technical accounting sense, gone.

I have raised a recovery with Brightwater and placed the vendor on payment hold so that no further Brightwater invoices go out until either the $1,280.00 comes back to us or we net it off against their March invoice. Their accounts person, who was pleasant, said they would "look into it," in the tone people use when they are already thinking about lunch. Dispute value: $1,280.00. I will chase on Monday.

I have also opened a ticket with IT to tighten the duplicate rule so it also flags vendor plus amount within a 30-day window regardless of invoice number. They have promised to "scope it." I await the scope with the patience of a saint and the mood of a tax auditor.

4. ORIEL SOFTWARE: A WARNING, NOT A HOLD

Oriel Software, who host the scheduling platform, sent their annual renewal invoice for $22,400.00. It matches the contract and the PO, and it is approved. It will be paid on its due date in April.

However, Oriel has now sent us three separate "friendly reminders" about this invoice, each with a 1.5% late fee helpfully pre-added, despite the invoice not being due until April and despite our contract with them explicitly excluding late fees. I have written to them explaining the concept of a due date. I have told their account manager that if they send one more invoice with an unauthorised late fee, I will put the account on hold until the billing team can demonstrate familiarity with a calendar.

To be clear: Oriel is not on hold. They have been warned. The warning was delivered with great restraint. You would have been proud. Or at least not embarrassed.

5. PELLHAM JANITORIAL: A PHONE CALL

Pellham Janitorial had one invoice this week, $2,340.00, matched and approved and paid on Thursday without drama. I spent forty minutes on hold with their billing office on Wednesday trying to get a W-9 refresh, which is due every three years and which they have now sent three times, each time with the previous year's address. The only hold involving Pellham this week was the one I was on, listening to a pan-flute rendition of a song I will not name because I do not want it back in my head. Pellham's account itself is clear and in good standing.

6. THE OTHER THREE DISPUTES

For completeness, the three disputes worth nobody's attention:

- Marrowgate Linens: $86.40, one missing box of patient bibs. Credit promised.
- Holloway Water Coolers: $44.00, a rental charged for a cooler we returned in January. Credit promised in January. Promised again in February. We may be here for some time.
- Fenwick Signage: $212.50, a sign spelled "Qiull Dental." They have agreed to reprint it. We have agreed not to put the misspelled one outside the Harrow Road clinic, although a small part of me wanted to.

None of these vendors is on hold; the amounts are small enough that we are paying the undisputed invoices normally and netting the credits off.

OPEN DISPUTES, SORTED BY DISPUTED AMOUNT

I know you like a table. Here is a table.

Vendor | Invoice total | Amount disputed | Status
Larkspur Rentals | $8,420.00 | $8,420.00 | On hold, corrected invoice requested
Tamsin Office Supply | $11,900.00 | $3,150.00 originally, now $0 | Credit note received, hold lifted Thu, closed
Brightwater Courier | $1,280.00 (paid twice) | $1,280.00 | Recovery raised, vendor on hold
Fenwick Signage | $212.50 | $212.50 | Reprint agreed
Marrowgate Linens | $86.40 | $86.40 | Credit promised
Holloway Water Coolers | $44.00 | $44.00 | Credit promised, allegedly

The other 21 invoices on hold are ordinary matching holds: missing receiving reports, mostly. I will spare you the list. The clinics involved have been emailed. Clinic 7 has been emailed twice. Clinic 7 knows what it did.

7. STAFFING

Now the part you will skim, so I have put it in plain words.

Volume is up. We received 214 invoices this week against a weekly average of 170 over the last quarter. Month end is in three weeks and quarter end with it. I have two AP clerks, one of whom, Lotte, is out for the last two weeks of March on long-planned leave that I approved in November, when I was younger and more optimistic.

You will remember that in December I asked for a second permanent clerk and the request was declined for budget reasons. I am not re-opening that. I accept that permanent headcount is not happening this year and I will stop mentioning it in meetings, mostly.

What I am asking for is narrower: I am formally requesting approval for one temporary AP clerk, through the agency we used last year, for four weeks starting 18 March, to cover Lotte's leave and quarter-end. Estimated cost is $6,800.00 based on last year's agency rate. I need an answer by Wednesday 13 March to get someone booked in time, because the agency needs three business days of notice and I would like the temp to arrive before the quarter does.

If the answer is no, the realistic consequence is that we miss the early-payment window on a handful of invoices and some of the matching holds sit longer than they should. I am not being dramatic. I am being arithmetic.

8. THINGS I AM NOT WORRIED ABOUT BUT YOU MIGHT HEAR ABOUT

- Someone in the east-side clinics has started a rumour that we have "stopped paying Larkspur forever." We have not. We have stopped paying one incorrect invoice and one duplicate until Larkspur sends a correct one. When they do, we will pay it. I have no personal grudge against Larkspur. Ines,

My preliminary view is as follows.

Exclusion 4.11 excludes loss 'caused directly or indirectly by any malicious act involving the unauthorised access to, use of, or interference with any computer system, network or software'. SP-4 does not write this back. Accordingly, if it were established that an outside party deliberately interfered with the controller and that this interference caused the compressors to stop, I would expect us to decline the spoilage claim under Exclusion 4.11.

However, a firewall label is not evidence of a malicious act. Automated systems frequently describe any burst of repeated connections as a denial of service event. The burden of establishing the exclusion rests with us, not with the insured. I would therefore recommend that you say nothing about the exclusion on site, that you obtain the insured's consent to a forensic examination of the controller, and that we instruct an independent firm. Harbor Analytics has done good work for us on industrial control systems before.

I would also suggest that we send a short reservation of rights letter once you have seen the site, so that the position is preserved while the investigation continues. I will prepare a draft. For clarity, a reservation of rights is not a declinature, and it should be framed so that the insured understands we are continuing to investigate in good faith.

6. The same installation reset the alarm configuration to factory defaults, in which high-temperature alarms are disabled.

We have found no evidence of access by any unauthorised party. We will provide our full summary by the end of the week.

Meeting: Site inspection, Riverton Distribution Centre, Cold Room 3
Date and time: Thursday, 14 March 2024, 10:00 to 12:40
Location: Riverton Distribution Centre, 400 Quayside Road; plant room and Cold Room 3
Present:
- Ines Sorensen, Senior Property Adjuster, Northmere Mutual (chair and note-taker)
- Callum Bergstrom, Director of Operations, Kestrel Foods

- Tomas Reyes, Facilities Manager, Kestrel Foods

- Oskar Valen, Senior Engineer, Coldline Services (refrigeration contractor)

1. Purpose of the meeting

Ms Sorensen explained that the purpose of the visit was to understand the circumstances of the temperature excursion, to inspect the refrigeration plant, controller and standby generator, and to agree next steps for the investigation. She stated that no view on coverage would be expressed at the meeting and that nothing said should be interpreted as acceptance or rejection of the claim.

2. Description of Cold Room 3

Mr Reyes described Cold Room 3 as a chilled storage room of approximately 1,100 square metres, served by three compressors on a common rack, controlled by a single Frostline RC-900 controller. The controller is connected to the site network so that it can report to the building management system and receive firmware updates. The design temperature range is 1 to 5 degrees Celsius. The room is used for dairy, prepared meals and fresh protein. Cold Rooms 1, 2 and 4 are served by separate racks and separate controllers of an older model, which are not network connected. Cold Rooms 1, 2 and 4 did not experience any excursion on 9 March 2024.

3. Sequence of events as understood by the insured

Mr Bergstrom summarised the insured's understanding. A storm passed through Riverton overnight on 8 to 9 March 2024. The utility has confirmed a mains interruption affecting the area. The insured initially assumed that the power outage caused the compressors to stop. At 06:15 the morning shift supervisor found the room at 11.8 degrees. However, Mr Moreau had already identified the problem at approximately 05:05 (see item 6).

4. Standby generator

Mr Reyes stated that the standby generator is a 400 kVA diesel unit which is tested monthly under load. The most recent test was on 1 March 2024 and was satisfactory. The generator's own log shows a start at 02:10:11 and a stop at 02:26:40 following retransfer to mains. Fuel level after the event was approximately 90 per cent. Ms Sorensen inspected the generator and its log display and photographed both. Mr Valen confirmed that the generator supplies the refrigeration racks for all four cold rooms.

Ms Sorensen observed that, if the generator carried the load throughout the interruption, the power outage alone would not explain why only Cold Room 3 failed, since the other three rooms, which are on the same generator, held temperature.

5. Refrigeration plant

Mr Valen had carried out a visual and audible inspection of the Cold Room 3 rack on 11 March 2024 without altering it. He reported that when the compressors were manually enabled at the local isolator for test purposes, all three started and ran. Compressor No. 2 produced bearing noise consistent with wear. In Mr Valen's opinion, the bearing wear is gradual and would have developed over many months. The compressor was nonetheless capable of running and cooling. In his opinion, the bearing wear did not cause the compressors to stop on 9 March 2024, and the rack would have maintained temperature on that night if the compressors had been enabled by the controller. He recommended replacement of the bearing within the next quarter as a maintenance matter.

Ms Sorensen asked whether there was any compressor failure on the night. Mr Valen replied that, in his view, there was no compressor failure in the sense of a mechanical breakdown; the compressors had simply not been asked to run.

6. Actions of the overnight operative (amended 15 March 2024)

Mr Moreau stated that he carried out his scheduled walk-round of all cold rooms at 03:00. Cold Room 3 was at 3.9 degrees and nothing appeared abnormal. His next scheduled walk-round was at 05:00. At approximately 05:05 he noticed that Cold Room 3 felt warm and that the local display read 9.6 degrees. He telephoned the on-call engineer at Coldline Services at 05:09 in accordance with the site procedure. There was no audible or visual high-temperature alarm at any point. Mr Moreau stated that he did not change any settings on the controller and did not have the password to do so.

(Amendment note: the original version of this item recorded that Mr Moreau did not respond to an alarm. That wording was incorrect and has been withdrawn at the insured's request. No alarm sounded.)

7. Controller and network

Ms Lind explained that the firewall had flagged repeated connection attempts involving the controller's network address between approximately 02:30 and 03:30, labelling them as a possible denial of service event. She had not yet been able to determine the origin. She confirmed that the controller is configured to accept firmware updates automatically from the manufacturer during a nightly maintenance window between 03:00 and 04:00. Ms Sorensen asked whether any updates had been received recently. Ms Lind was unsure.

Ms Sorensen explained that Northmere Mutual would like to instruct an independent forensic firm to examine the controller and network records, and asked the insured to preserve the controller and not to reboot or reconfigure it. Ms Lind agreed.

8. Stock and quality assurance

Mr Bergstrom explained that the insured's food safety procedure requires chilled products exposed to more than 8 degrees for more than two hours to be destroyed unless they fall within a list of exempt product types, which includes certain hard cheeses and sealed long-life products. Quality assurance assessment was in progress. Destruction of non-exempt stock was scheduled through Greenway Waste. Ms Sorensen inspected the quarantined stock and took photographs.

9. Mitigation

Mr Bergstrom confirmed that refrigerated trailers had been hired from 11 March 2024 to maintain incoming and outgoing deliveries. Ms Sorensen confirmed that reasonable steps to reduce the loss were expected and that invoices should be retained.

10. Next steps

- Northmere Mutual to instruct Harbor Analytics (subject to insured's consent).
- Insured to provide written consent and nominate an IT contact.
- Insured to retain stock, destruction and trailer records.
- Coldline Services not to alter controller or compressor units pending forensic examination.
- Ms Sorensen to circulate these notes.

ATTACHMENT C: SUMMARY OF FORENSIC FINDINGS, HARBOR ANALYTICS
======================================================================

Prepared for: Northmere Mutual (instructing party) and Kestrel Foods Ltd.
Prepared by: Dmitri Haddad, Principal Investigator, Harbor Analytics
Date: Friday, 29 March 2024
Matter: NM-CL-2024-0817, Riverton Cold Room 3

C1. Scope

Harbor Analytics was instructed to determine, so far as possible from the available records and equipment, why the compressors serving Cold Room 3 stopped running on 9 March 2024, and in particular whether any of the following contributed: (i) the mains interruption; (ii) any failure of the standby generator; (iii) any unauthorised access to or interference with the controller; (iv) any mechanical failure of the compressors; (v) any action of site personnel.

C2. Materials examined

Forensic image of the Frostline RC-900 controller, including event log, configuration store and firmware partitions; firewall logs for FW-EDGE-01 for 1 to 13 March 2024; building management system export for 8 to 9 March 2024; generator control panel log; Coldline Services inspection notes of 11 March 2024; interviews with Ms Lind, Mr Reyes and Mr Moreau; the manufacturer's release notes for firmware 4.2.1 and its subsequent service bulletin.

C3. Mains interruption and generator

The mains interruption lasted from 02:10:03 to 02:24:31, a period of fourteen minutes and twenty-eight seconds. The generator started at 02:10:11 and carried all refrigeration loads until retransfer at 02:26:40. The controller log records continuous uptime across the event. Cold Room 3 temperature remained between 2.8 and 3.0 degrees during and after the interruption. We find that neither the mains interruption nor the generator was the cause of the compressor stoppage. The mains interruption had one indirect effect, discussed at C4: it briefly interrupted the site's internet uplink, which interrupted the controller's first attempt to download an available firmware package.

C4. Firewall alerts

The firewall recorded three alerts categorised as 'possible_DoS' between 02:36 and 03:15. All of the associated traffic was outbound, initiated by the controller itself (10.20.4.17), and directed to the manufacturer's update distribution host. The traffic pattern is consistent with the controller's update client retrying a failed download at a high rate, which the manufacturer has since acknowledged as a defect in its retry logic. There was no inbound traffic to the controller from any external address during the period. Authentication logs on the controller show no remote login between 1 and 9 March 2024; the only interactive login on 9 March 2024 was the local login by the Coldline engineer at 05:48. We find no evidence of unauthorised access, malicious interference or any attack by an outside party. The 'possible_DoS' label reflects the firewall's generic rate-threshold rule and does not indicate that an attack took place.

C5. Firmware installation and its effect

The controller downloaded firmware version 4.2.1 at 03:27 and installed it at 03:30 to 03:31 during its configured automatic maintenance window. During installation, the configuration migration routine converted the existing setpoint, alarm and schedule tables to a new format. For controllers with three-circuit racks configured under version 4.1.7, the migration routine wrote null values to the setpoint table and reverted the alarm profile to factory default. The manufacturer's service bulletin FSB-2024-07, issued on 21 March 2024, confirms this behaviour and withdraws version 4.2.1.

Under the controller's logic, a null setpoint places the circuit in defrost hold, in which the compressors are held off. Accordingly, from 03:32 the controller held all three compressors off while continuing to report a 'heartbeat OK' status. Because the factory default alarm profile disables the high-temperature alarm, no alarm was raised as the room warmed.

We find that the stoppage of the compressors was caused by the corrupted setpoint configuration written by the controller's own firmware installation, and that the absence of an alarm was caused by the same installation.

C6. Compressors

We reviewed the Coldline Services notes and the controller's run records. Each compressor ran normally until 03:32 and each responded normally when placed in manual run at 05:52. Compressor No. 2 exhibits bearing wear consistent with gradual deterioration. This wear did not prevent the compressor from running and did not contribute to the stoppage. We find no compressor failure on 9 March 2024.

C7. Site personnel

There is no evidence that any member of site staff altered controller settings. Mr Moreau's walk-rounds at 03:00 and 05:00 were in accordance with the site procedure, and his report at 05:09 was prompt. Given that the high-temperature alarm had been disabled by the firmware installation, we do not consider that any operator error contributed to the loss.

C8. Conclusion

The compressors serving Cold Room 3 were held off from 03:32 to 05:52 on 9 March 2024 because the controller's automatic installation of firmware version 4.2.1 corrupted its setpoint table and reset its alarm profile. The mains interruption, the standby generator, the firewall alerts, the condition of the compressors and the actions of site staff were not causes of the stoppage.

C9. Fees

Our fees for this instruction are 9,600, invoiced to Northmere Mutual.

======================================================================

Meeting: Coverage review, claim NM-CL-2024-0817
Date: Tuesday, 2 April 2024, 14:00 to 15:10
Location: Northmere Mutual, Claims Floor, Meeting Room 6 (with video link)
Present:
- Ines Sorensen, Senior Property Adjuster (chair)
- Mateo Novak, Coverage Counsel
- Rhea Castell, Claims Technical Manager
- Jonas Pike, Claims Accounts
Note-taker: Jonas Pike

D1. Background

Ms Sorensen summarised the claim, the site visit and the Harbor Analytics findings. The insured has claimed a total of 267,350 across six items, subsequently reduced by 4,400 in respect of released stock.

D2. Exclusion 4.11 (malicious computer interference)

Mr Novak advised that, in light of section C4 of the Harbor Analytics summary, there is no basis for relying on Exclusion 4.11. The exclusion requires a malicious act involving unauthorised access or interference. The firewall alerts were generated by the controller's own outbound update traffic and there was no unauthorised access. The draft declinature letter that he had prepared on 20 March 2024 as a contingency, in case the forensic investigation established a cyberattack, was never sent and is now withdrawn. Mr Novak asked that the file record clearly that no declinature under Exclusion 4.11 has been or will be issued.

Ms Castell asked whether a software defect could itself fall within Exclusion 4.11. Mr Novak advised that it could not; a defect in the manufacturer's firmware is not a malicious act by anyone, and the exclusion is not engaged. He noted that the base policy contains no general exclusion for software faults, and that SP-4 expressly covers spoilage resulting from 'failure or malfunction of refrigeration equipment, including its controls'. A controller that holds the compressors off because of corrupted configuration is a malfunction of the equipment's controls.

D3. Exclusion 4.3 (wear and tear)

The meeting agreed that Exclusion 4.3 does not apply to the spoilage, since the bearing wear on Compressor No. 2 did not cause the loss. However, the cost of replacing the worn bearing is not itself a loss caused by the insured event. It is a maintenance cost for gradual deterioration, which is excluded by Exclusion 4.3 and in any event was not caused by the occurrence. Item 4 (8,400) is therefore not payable.

D4. Item 1: destroyed stock

Claimed 187,300. Reduced by released stock of 4,400 as notified by the insured on 29 March 2024. Adjusted figure: 187,300 minus 4,400 equals 182,900. Destruction certificates reconcile to this figure. Payable at 182,900. Within the spoilage sublimit of 250,000.

D5. Item 2: disposal

Claimed 6,200. Greenway Waste invoices reconcile. SP-4 covers the cost of removing and disposing of spoiled stock. Payable at 6,200.

D6. Item 3: trailer hire and freight

Claimed 14,850. Ms Castell asked whether this item represented business interruption, which is not covered. Ms Sorensen explained that the trailers were hired to protect stock that would otherwise have spoiled in Cold Room 3 while it was out of service pending forensic examination, which falls within the expediting expense provision of SP-4. Mr Novak agreed. Payable at 14,850.

D7. Item 5: lost gross profit

Claimed 41,000. The insured did not purchase the Business Income extension. SP-4 covers the physical loss of stock and specified expenses only; it does not cover loss of profit or loss of revenue. Although Item 3 has been accepted as an expediting expense, that does not bring lost profit within cover. Item 5 is not payable.

D8. Item 6: forensic fees

Harbor Analytics fees of 9,600, recorded within the settlement under the claim preparation provision of SP-4 (limit 10,000) per Ms Sorensen's message of 27 March 2024. Payable at 9,600, settled directly with Harbor Analytics.

D9. Settlement computation

Mr Pike presented the computation:
Item 1: 182,900
Item 2: 6,200
Item 3: 14,850
Item 6: 9,600
Subtotal of accepted items: 182,900 + 6,200 + 14,850 + 9,600 = 213,550
Less deductible: 10,000
Net settlement: 203,550
Of which paid to Harbor Analytics: 9,600
Of which payable to the insured: 193,950

Items not accepted: Item 4 (8,400) and Item 5 (41,000), total 49,400.

D10. Recovery

Mr Novak advised that Northmere Mutual should consider a subrogated recovery against the controller manufacturer in light of service bulletin FSB-2024-07. The insured should be asked to preserve the controller and the withdrawn firmware image.

D11. Actions

- Ms Sorensen to issue the coverage position letter accepting the claim in part, with reasons for the items not accepted.
- Mr Novak to open a recovery file.
- Mr Pike to prepare payment on receipt of signed proof of loss.

POSTMORTEM: INC-2291 - Misrouted shipping labels at Larkspur Outfitters Reno Distribution Center
Author: Farid Moreau (Platform Reliability, Larkspur Outfitters)
Reviewers: Leila Kaur (DC Operations), Jonas Mensah (Integrations)
Status: Final, blameless format, as blameless as a document can be when a cron job is involved
Incident date: Tuesday, 14 October
Document date: Tuesday, 21 October

1. SUMMARY

On Tuesday 14 October, the label-generation service we license from Harbor Software returned incorrect routing codes for outbound parcels from the Reno Distribution Center. From 09:12 to 12:47 Pacific, every parcel label printed at the pack stations had a correctly formatted barcode that pointed to the wrong sort hub. The labels were beautiful. They scanned perfectly. They were simply wrong, which is the kind of failure that monitoring dashboards find deeply unremarkable.

In total, 1,284 parcels were labeled during the affected window. Of these, 1,279 were caught at the outbound dock before trailers departed. Five parcels left the building on the 11:30 regional trailer before the hold was issued. All five were located and handled; see Section 5 and Appendix A for the reconciliation, which I encourage everyone to read, if only because it is the one part of this document with a happy ending.

The root cause was a scheduled zone-table import job in the Harbor Software integration layer that loaded a staging test file instead of the production zone table. The job reported success, because technically it did succeed. It successfully imported the wrong thing.

2. IMPACT

- 1,284 parcels labeled with incorrect sort-hub routing codes.
- 1,279 parcels relabeled on site between 12:50 and 17:40.
- 5 parcels departed on trailer RNO-1130 before the hold. Status of each is in Appendix A.
- Approximately 3 hours 35 minutes of degraded label service (09:12 to 12:47).
- Roughly 46 labor-hours of relabeling across two shifts. Leila Kaur estimates the emotional labor-hours as "uncountable."
- Customer-facing impact: 212 orders showed a delayed ship date on the storefront. Customer service received 37 contacts, 31 of which were polite, which exceeds our historical average.
- No customer data was exposed, altered or accessed by any unauthorized party. More on that in Section 4, because someone will ask.

The label service was never fully unavailable. It responded to every request within normal latency. Our uptime monitor, which checks that the service returns HTTP 200 and a PDF, stayed a reassuring green throughout. It remains green in spirit today.

3. TIMELINE (all times Pacific, 14 October unless noted)

02:00 - Scheduled job zone_sync_nightly begins in the Harbor Software integration container. It pulls the zone table from the file path configured in the environment variable ZONE_SOURCE.

02:03 - Job completes. Log line: "Imported 4,118 zone rows. Status OK." The production table has 4,406 rows. Nobody is awake to notice that 4,118 is a smaller number than 4,406, and in fairness, the job did not mention it either.

06:00 - First shift starts at the Reno DC. Pack stations 1 through 22 online. Labels printed between 06:00 and 09:11 use the cached zone table from the previous day, because the cache TTL is seven hours. This will become relevant.

09:12 - Label cache expires and the service begins reading from the newly imported staging table. First mis-routed label printed at pack station 7. It looks identical to every other label.

09:40 - An outbound dock associate notes that the sort code on a parcel bound for Boise reads "SLC-3" rather than the usual "BOI-1." The associate assumes the carrier changed routing. This is a reasonable assumption given how often carriers change routing without telling us.

10:05 - Carrier pickup for trailer RNO-1000 is loaded. This trailer contains only parcels labeled before 09:12 plus a batch of returns being consolidated. Later verification confirmed none of the 1,284 affected parcels were on RNO-1000.

10:22 - Customer service receives the first contact asking why an order placed Monday shows a ship date of Thursday. Unrelated: that order was backordered. We note it here because it consumed eleven minutes of investigation and we want credit for thoroughness.

10:58 - Jonas Mensah, reviewing an unrelated integration ticket, notices the zone table row count in the admin panel reads 4,118. He writes in the integrations channel: "Is it normal for the zone table to lose 288 rows overnight or is that a vibe?" Nobody answers for fourteen minutes, because it is Tuesday.

11:12 - Jonas opens a ticket with Harbor Software support (HS-55810), severity 2.

11:30 - Trailer RNO-1130 departs with 1,402 parcels, of which 5 were labeled during the affected window. The other 1,397 were labeled before 09:12 or were non-label freight (pallets with manually printed BOLs).

11:44 - Leila Kaur, walking the outbound dock, sees three consecutive parcels for Portland labeled for the Salt Lake hub. She stops the line at dock door 4 and asks the dock lead to check the others. The dock lead reports "a lot of them" are wrong. We have since quantified "a lot" as 1,279.

11:51 - Leila issues an outbound hold for all doors. Trailer RNO-1200 is held at the dock with doors open.

12:02 - Incident declared. Farid Moreau assumes incident commander role. Bridge opened.

12:10 - Harbor Software support upgrades HS-55810 to severity 1 at our request. Their engineer on call confirms the zone table checksum does not match production.

12:26 - Jonas identifies that ZONE_SOURCE in the integration container points to /data/zones/staging/zones_test_v3.csv. A deployment the previous Friday copied an environment file from the staging container to production. The staging file had been sitting there waiting for exactly this opportunity.

12:38 - Corrected ZONE_SOURCE value deployed. Manual run of zone_sync_nightly started.

12:44 - Import completes. Log line: "Imported 4,406 zone rows. Status OK." The job's enthusiasm is unchanged from 02:03.

12:47 - Label cache flushed. First correct label printed at pack station 3. Degraded window ends.

12:50 - Relabeling begins. Leila organizes relabeling by dock door. Pack stations are reassigned to reprint labels from the order management system by scanning the old label.

13:15 - Farid contacts the carrier's regional desk about trailer RNO-1130 and requests intercept of the five affected parcels.

14:30 - Carrier confirms all five parcels identified by tracking number at the Salt Lake hub, where they were sorted according to the incorrect labels. Two are shown in the carrier portal with a status of "LOST - SEARCH IN PROGRESS" for reasons nobody at the carrier could explain on the phone.

15:40 - Carrier updates the two "LOST" parcels to "LOCATED - EXCEPTION HOLD." Carrier rep explains that parcels with sort codes that do not match their destination ZIP are automatically flagged as lost after two failed scans. So the parcels were lost in the sense that the software could not believe where they were, which is relatable.

17:40 - Relabeling complete. 1,279 parcels relabeled and verified by second scan. Outbound hold lifted.

18:05 - Trailer RNO-1200 departs, four hours and fifty-five minutes late.

15 October, 09:00 - Carrier reroutes three of the five RNO-1130 parcels from Salt Lake to correct destinations. The other two are returned to Reno at customer's request for reshipment with expedited service (see Appendix A).

17 October, 16:20 - Final of the five parcels delivered. Reconciliation closed.

4. ROOT CAUSE AND WHAT WE RULED OUT

The root cause was configuration drift: a production environment file overwritten by a staging environment file during a routine deployment on Friday 10 October. The Friday deployment was reviewed and approved. The reviewer checked the diff of the application code. The environment file was not in the diff, because the deploy script copies it separately. This is the kind of detail that is obvious in hindsight and invisible in foresight, like most of the Reno parking lot signage.

Because several people have asked, and because the initial Slack speculation was lively, here is what the incident was not:

4.1 Warehouse hardware. During the incident, several people suspected the label printers or handheld scanners. Pack stations 7 and 12 had been flagged the previous week for printhead wear. We checked: every printer produced labels that were printed correctly according to the data it received. Every scanner read every barcode correctly. The hardware did exactly what it was told, which in this case was the wrong thing. No hardware fault contributed to the incident. The printhead replacement on stations 7 and 12 is still scheduled, as it was before, for unrelated reasons.

4.2 Carrier systems. At 11:12 one theory was that the carrier had pushed a routing change on their side. The carrier's API status page showed no incidents on 14 October, and their regional desk confirmed no routing table updates that week. The carrier's systems correctly routed parcels according to the labels they were given. The "LOST" status on two parcels was a consequence of our bad labels, not an outage or defect on their side. The carrier is not a contributing cause, although they have asked us to note that they would appreciate labels that point to the right city.

4.3 Security. Someone on the bridge at 12:15 asked whether this could be a malicious change. Jonas and our security team reviewed the deploy logs, the container access logs and the Harbor Software audit trail. The environment file change came from our own deploy pipeline, triggered by an approved merge, under a service account used for every deployment. There was no unauthorized access, no credential misuse and no evidence of tampering. The staging test file was created by a Harbor Software engineer in August for a load test and is exactly what it claims to be: a test file with 288 fewer rows and a sense of humor.

4.4 Dock and pack staff. The pack stations printed labels from order data they did not enter manually; no associate typed or selected a routing code at any point. Dock associates loaded parcels as labeled. The associate who noticed the Boise anomaly at 09:40 did not escalate, but our dock procedure at that time did not require escalation for sort-code changes, and the procedure has since been updated (Action item 6). No staff member entered incorrect data or deviated from the procedure as written. Leila has asked that this section be read aloud at the next all-hands. We are considering it.

4.5 The zone_sync_nightly job itself. The job code worked as designed: it imports whatever file it is pointed at. It has no row-count validation and no checksum comparison against the previous day. That is a gap in design, addressed in Action items 1 and 2, rather than a bug.

Contributing factors:
- Deploy script copies environment files outside the reviewed diff.
- Staging test data stored in a path reachable from the production container.
- Import job has no sanity checks.
- Uptime monitor checks availability, not correctness.
- Seven-hour cache TTL delayed the onset until peak shift, which is the least convenient possible moment and therefore, statistically, the most likely.

5. RECOVERY AND RECONCILIATION

All 1,284 affected parcels are accounted for. The 1,279 held on site were relabeled and shipped on 14 October on trailers RNO-1200 (departed 18:05) and RNO-1830 (departed 19:12). The five on RNO-1130 were intercepted at the Salt Lake hub. Three were rerouted by the carrier and delivered on 15 and 16 October. Two were returned to Reno at the customers' request and reshipped with expedited service; both were delivered, the last on 17 October.

The temporary "LOST - SEARCH IN PROGRESS" status on two parcels was cleared by the carrier within about 70 minutes. We have asked the carrier to add a note to the tracking history so the customers do not see the word "LOST" and draw the natural conclusion. They have agreed to consider it, which in carrier terms is a firm commitment.

No parcels were declared lost, no carrier claims were filed and no replacement orders were created for loss. Customer service issued goodwill shipping-fee refunds on 19 orders, totaling $142.50, for delay only. These are listed in Appendix A.

6. SERVICE LEVEL ASSESSMENT (Harbor Software contract)

Our agreement with Harbor Software (Master Services Agreement, Schedule C) provides service credits as follows. Quoting Schedule C, clause 4:

"Service Credits apply where Severity 1 Degradation or Unavailability of the Label Service, measured from the time the incident is reported to Harbor Software or first detected by Harbor Software monitoring, whichever is earlier, until restoration, exceeds in aggregate two hundred forty (240) minutes within a single calendar month. Credits are calculated on the monthly subscription fee: aggregate 241 to 480 minutes: 5%; 481 to 960 minutes: 10%; more than 960 minutes: 15%. Periods of degradation not reported to or detected by Harbor Software are excluded."

For INC-2291, Harbor Software did not detect the issue through their monitoring. We reported it at 11:12 (ticket HS-55810). Service was restored at 12:47. The countable period is therefore 11:12 to 12:47, which is 95 minutes. Our internal degraded window of 09:12 to 12:47 (215 minutes) would also not exceed 240 minutes even if the whole window counted, which it does not.

There were no other Harbor Software Severity 1 incidents in October. The 40-minute Harbor Software outage on 29 September (INC-2240) falls in the previous calendar month and does not aggregate with October. September's total was 40 minutes, also below the threshold.

Jonas has noted that the relabeling labor (approximately 46 labor-hours) and the goodwill refunds ($142.50) are not recoverable under Schedule C, which covers only subscription credits. Our contract team has confirmed there is no separate indemnity for data errors. Harbor Software has offered, in writing, a "root cause review session" at no charge. We have accepted, on the basis that it costs nothing, which is also its likely value.

Conclusion: the service-credit threshold in Schedule C was not met for October, and no service credit tier applies to INC-2291.

7. WHAT WENT WELL

- Leila's walk of the outbound dock caught the issue before a second full trailer departed. The process that caught the issue was, technically, Leila getting her steps in.
- Relabeling was organized quickly and verified with a second scan on every parcel.
- The carrier's regional desk located all five departed parcels within about 75 minutes of our request.
- Harbor Software support escalated promptly once asked and identified the checksum mismatch within eight minutes.

8. WHAT WENT POORLY

- 106 minutes elapsed between the first mis-routed label and anyone noticing the row-count drop.
- The 09:40 anomaly was seen and rationalized. Our procedures encouraged this rationalization.
- Our uptime monitor was green throughout. We have monitoring that confirms the service is alive, and no monitoring that confirms it is telling the truth.
- The incident bridge spent roughly twenty minutes on hardware and security theories that the evidence did not support. Enthusiasm is not a diagnostic method.

9. ACTION ITEMS

1. Add row-count validation to zone_sync_nightly: fail and alert if the imported row count differs from the previous day's by more than 1%. Owner: Jonas Mensah. Due 31 October.
2. Add checksum comparison against a signed production manifest. Owner: Jonas Mensah with Harbor Software. Due 14 November.
3. Move staging test data out of any path mounted in production containers. Owner: Harbor Software (tracked in HS-55811). Due 7 November.
4. Change deploy script to include environment files in the reviewed diff. Owner: Farid Moreau. Due 31 October.
5. Add a synthetic label-correctness check: every 15 minutes, request labels for ten known addresses and compare sort codes to expected values. Owner: Farid Moreau. Due 7 November.
6. Update dock procedure to require escalation to the shift lead for any sort code that differs from the usual code for a destination. Owner: Leila Kaur. Completed 17 October.
7. Reduce label cache TTL from seven hours to one hour. Owner: Jonas Mensah. Due 24 October. Note: this will not prevent a bad import, it will just make us find out sooner, which is the point.
